title: API keys: what they are and how not to leak them
promise: You're going to get a key and store it where no one can see it. You're going to check with your own eyes that it doesn't travel to the internet. And you're going to know how to rotate it in three minutes the day it escapes.
why: Diego built a website for his surf school in Conil with ChatGPT: a chat that answered questions about schedules and prices. It worked perfectly, and he published it on a Thursday. By Sunday he had $1,900 in charges on his OpenAI account. The key was written inside the page, so anyone who opened the site could see it in two keystrokes. And it wasn't found by a hacker in a hoodie. It was found by an automated program that spends the whole day scanning the internet for exactly that. What would have saved him wasn't knowing how to code: it was knowing where a key does NOT go.

theory.title: A key isn't a password: it's a house key with your credit card taped to it
theory.text: An API key is the password one program uses to talk to another program. It's a string of letters and numbers, something like sk-ant-api03-J9xK7mQ2 plus ninety more characters. It looks like a password, but it works in a much more dangerous way. When you log into your bank they ask for a username, a password, and a code sent to your phone: three things. The key doesn't ask for any of that, because it's username, password, and code all in the same string. Whoever holds it is you, as far as OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google are concerned. There's no second question and no warning email. Nobody ever asks you "is that really you logging in from Vietnam at four in the morning?" You might be thinking that's a design flaw, and it isn't. It's built that way on purpose, so a program can use it a thousand times a minute in the middle of the night with no one there to confirm anything. The price of that convenience is that storing it safely is one hundred percent your responsibility. And there's no "that wasn't me" button.
theory.analogy: It's a hotel key card that also has the minibar and the restaurant unlocked. Whoever finds it dropped in the hallway walks into the room and orders lobster for eight, and the bill lands on your name. The door doesn't check faces: it only reads the card.
theory.example: The prefixes give away who each key belongs to. Anthropic's start with sk-ant-api03-. OpenAI's, with sk-proj-. Google's, with AIza. Stripe's, which move real money, with sk_live_. Those prefixes aren't decoration: they're exactly what the programs scanning the internet look for. At a glance they tell them what they've found and which company's account to go spend it on.

theory.title: The bots that scan for them, and why they're coming for yours
theory.text: There are automated programs (bots, programs that work alone, with no one watching) dedicated to a single task: sweeping the internet for those text strings. They're not looking for you. They sweep all of GitHub, freshly published websites, forums, Discord channels, and screenshots uploaded to public sites. The speed is what's dizzying. A public repository is a folder of code stored on the internet. In published experiments, a key uploaded to one of them got its first use in under a minute. And that use came from an unknown location. Not hours, not days: less time than it takes you to realize what you just did. The volume is scary too. GitGuardian is a company dedicated precisely to this. In its annual report it counted more than twenty million new keys exposed in public GitHub repositories in 2024 alone. And they do it because it's a business. Access to the good models gets resold cheap, in markets where hundreds of people use your key at once. If you're thinking "nobody cares about my project," you're completely right and it makes no difference at all. They're not looking for your project, they're looking for the text string. It's all the same to them whether there's a San Francisco company behind it or a surf school's schedule page.
theory.example: The bill never arrives with the word "theft" written on it. It arrives like this: some random Tuesday you open the console and see $340 in charges from the night before. The requests are from 4:12, 4:12, and 4:13 in the morning, in Chinese, in Russian, and in Portuguese. And you have eight users, and all eight live in Cadiz.

theory.title: The five places it leaks from, and the fourth doesn't look like a mistake
theory.text: One: pasting it into the chat box so the AI can "use it." It doesn't need it to write the code. And there it stays, saved in a conversation that can be shared with a link, exported, or sit in your history for years. Two: the AI writes it directly into the code, in the middle of a file. This happens because you gave it to it, or because it copied it from an example. Three: uploading the project folder to GitHub with the keys file inside. Lots of people do this without knowing that anything uploaded there in public mode can be read by anyone. Four, and this is the one that sinks people. The key ends up in the part of your site that downloads entirely to every visitor's computer. This fourth one throws no error, triggers no alert, and your site works beautifully. Meanwhile anyone who visits can press F12, search for "sk-", and have your key on screen in six seconds without knowing how to code. Five: the screenshot you upload to a forum asking for help with an error, with the key peeking out on a line in the background. Or the public link to the conversation that you send a friend. All five have the same fix, and you're going to set it up in this lesson's tasks.
theory.analogy: The other four are leaving the key in different places. The fourth is making copies of the key. And handing them out, one by one and with a smile, to everyone who's walked into your store.
theory.example: Diego, from the surf school, fell into the fourth one. His key was in a file called script.js. Every visitor's browser downloaded that entire file so the site would work. Any of the 200 visitors that week could have pressed F12, gone to the "Sources" tab, and read it. A bot read it before any person did.

theory.title: Where a well-kept key lives: .env and .gitignore
theory.text: The solution isn't to hide the key better inside the code: it's to take it out of the code. This is done with a file called .env (for "environment"). It's a plain text document that lives in your project folder with one line per key, like this: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-whatever. No quotes and no spaces around the equals sign, which is the most repeated mistake of all. The code stops carrying the key and starts carrying just the name: "grab whatever is stored in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY." For that file to never travel, you need a second file, the .gitignore. It's the list of things that don't get uploaded to the internet, and it needs to contain a line with .env, written exactly like that. It's paired with a .env.example, the same list of names but with the values left blank. That way, three months from now you'll know which keys the project needed without having to guess. And when you publish the real website, the keys don't travel with the files. You paste them by hand into the panel of the service hosting it, in a section called "Environment Variables." There's one trap left, and it's an expensive one. Any variable whose name starts with NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ gets sent to the browser on purpose, by design. So if your AI writes NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENAI_API_KEY, your key is published even if it's safely tucked in the .env.
theory.analogy: The .env is your house's safe. The code is a note stuck on the fridge that says "it's in the safe." You can show the note to anyone, because it's useless without the safe. What you were doing before was writing the whole combination on the note and hanging it on the front door.
theory.example: The names with a dangerous prefix are exactly the ones AIs propose when they're in a hurry. They're the ones that make things work on the first try. VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY works perfectly on Tuesday and on Thursday you have $600 in charges. OPENAI_API_KEY, with no prefix, forces the call to move to the server: more work that afternoon, and it saves you the whole scare.

theory.title: Rotating: the only fix that exists
theory.text: If a key has been seen, even for a second, it's burned. It doesn't matter if it was in a screenshot you deleted right away. Deleting it from the file doesn't unburn it: it's still valid on the company's servers, and whoever copied it can still use it tonight. With GitHub it's even worse, because it keeps every previous version of every file. You delete the line, push the change, and the site looks clean. But the key is still in there, in the history, two clicks away from anyone, forever. The only fix that works is called rotating, and it's two moves: create a new key and delete the old one. What actually fixes the problem is the second half, because creating a new one without deleting the old one fixes absolutely nothing. It's free, takes two minutes, and there's no limit on how many times you can do it. And nobody finds out: no notice goes out, no mark is left on your account, and there's no one to explain yourself to. Order does matter here, and this step is irreversible. Create the new one, paste it in the right place, check that everything still works, and only then delete the old one. The second you delete it, anything still using it stops working. And sometimes they rotate it for you. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have an arrangement with GitHub to be notified when one of their keys shows up in a public repository. They disable it themselves and send you an email. That email isn't spam, it's the best news possible: it means they got there before the bot did.
theory.example: Marina realized at 11:40 PM that she'd accidentally pushed her .env to GitHub. By 11:42 she had a new key created at console.anthropic.com. By 11:44 she'd pasted it into the Vercel panel. At 11:45 she clicked the button to delete the old one. Total cost of the leak: $0.00. If she'd gone to bed thinking she'd fix it in the morning, she'd have paid for a whole night of someone else's usage.

theory.title: The spending cap: the safety net for when everything else fails
theory.text: Everything above can fail, because you're new and you're going to make mistakes. The spending cap is what turns a catastrophe into a $10 scare. There are two opposite settings that people constantly confuse. Auto-recharge is the dangerous one: you're telling the company "when I drop below $5, charge me $20 more." One night with a loop or a bot inside drains your card in $20 installments while you sleep. The safe one is prepay: you put in $10 and when it runs out, it's out. The program stops working and returns a 429 or a 402 error, and it stopping working is exactly what you want to happen. If you're thinking "what if it runs out in the middle of something important?", the answer is simple. You'd rather be stuck for twenty minutes on a Thursday night than wake up to $1,900. To learn you don't even need a card: Google AI Studio has a free tier where you can run hundreds of tests for $0. And with $10 of prepaid credit on Anthropic or OpenAI you have weeks of real practice. Just one thing: don't leave any program running unattended overnight.
theory.example: For Diego, a spending cap would have cost him an annoyed Friday morning seeing his site had stopped. Without a spending cap, it cost him $1,900. The difference between the two stories is two checkboxes you touch in four minutes, before writing a single line of code.

tasks.title: Ask the AI which keys your idea actually needs
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini text box
tasks.action: Open a new conversation and paste the prompt below with the blank filled in. Don't get any key yet. The goal of this task is to avoid ending up with six accounts and cards set up for a project that needs just one key, or none. Read the whole answer before touching anything.
tasks.prompt:
You're a software architect who works with people who can't code and who hates unnecessary spending.

My idea is this:
[DESCRIBE YOUR IDEA IN TWO OR THREE LINES: WHAT IT DOES, WHO IT'S FOR, AND WHAT HAPPENS WHEN SOMEONE USES IT]

I want to build the first version, the smallest one I could show someone. Tell me this and nothing else:

1) Which API keys I actually need for THAT first version. If the answer is none, say so and explain why.
2) For each key: the company name, the exact web address where you get it, whether it requires a credit card or not, whether it has a free tier, and roughly how much I'll spend in dollars the first month testing it.
3) Which of those keys I can leave for later without the first version stopping working.
4) Which of those keys move money or delete data, so I treat them more carefully than the rest.

Order them from least dangerous to most dangerous. Don't suggest a paid service if there's a free one that does the same thing to start with. Don't explain yet how to code anything. Answer me in a table, plainly, no fluff.
tasks.expect: A short list, usually one to three keys. For each one it'll tell you the company name, the exact address where you get it, and whether it needs a card. With luck, a line telling you that you don't need any to get started.
tasks.stuck: If it hands you a list of eight services with a database, a payment gateway, and an analytics system, reply: "this is the final version. Tell me only what I need for the dumbest possible first version, the one that only has to run for me on my own computer." It usually drops from eight to one.

tasks.title: Get your first key in Google AI Studio, free and with no card
tasks.action: Log in with your usual Google account. You'll see a blue button that says "Create API key." If it asks which project to put it in, choose "Create API key in new project." That way you don't have to decide anything. The key appears in a box with a copy icon next to it. Copy it right then, don't wait. As soon as you close that box, most services only show you the last four characters and there's no way to get the rest back. And don't paste it into any AI's chat: it goes straight into the password manager in the next task.
tasks.expect: A string that starts with AIza followed by about thirty-five more characters. And almost always a warning not to share it or that you won't see it in full again.
tasks.stuck: If it starts talking about enabling billing or Google Cloud, you've landed in the Cloud console instead of AI Studio. Type aistudio.google.com/apikey into the address bar by hand again, without searching for it on Google. If the button doesn't show up, try an incognito window. Having several Google accounts open at once breaks this screen quite often.

tasks.title: Save it in your password manager before closing the tab
tasks.where: In your password manager: Chrome's, Apple Keychain, Bitwarden, or 1Password
tasks.action: If you don't have one, Bitwarden is free and works fine. Create a new entry of type "secure note." Give it a title with three pieces of info: which key it is, which project, and the date. For example: "Gemini key — surf school site — created 08/19/2026." Paste the key into the body. That date isn't decoration. Six months from now you'll have four similar keys in the list. The date will be the only thing that tells you which one to delete. Don't store it in your phone's Notes app, a Word document, an email to yourself, or a WhatsApp message. Those four places sync on their own, get shared by accident, and end up open in front of someone else.
tasks.expect: An entry in your password manager with the full title and the key inside, and the Google AI Studio tab closed without any fear.
tasks.stuck: If you already closed the tab without copying it, you haven't broken anything. Go back to aistudio.google.com/apikey, delete the key you just lost with the trash icon, and create another one. It's thirty seconds and costs no money. It's exactly the same move you'll make the day a real one leaks, so treat this as a first rehearsal.

tasks.title: Set the spending cap and turn off auto-recharge
tasks.where: In your browser, at platform.openai.com and console.anthropic.com
tasks.action: This only applies if you've ever entered a card on either of the two. Log in with your account and find the "Billing" section, usually inside "Settings." First look for the "Auto recharge" checkbox and leave it off: that's the one that can drain your card in installments while you sleep. Then look for "Limits" or "Budgets" and set a monthly cap of $10 and an email alert at $5. If you've never entered a card in either one, you're already done with this task. You have no open doors, and that's the safest state there is.
tasks.expect: Auto-recharge off and a number written into the monthly cap. Take a screenshot of that screen for yourself, because these panels move around every few months and you won't find anything later.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the section, type the word "limit" into the site's own search box. If it tells you you need to be an org admin, you're inside someone else's or a company's account. Get out of there and create your own before continuing.

tasks.title: Have the AI set up the .env and the .gitignore
tasks.where: In the text box of the AI you're building your project with
tasks.action: Paste the prompt below in the conversation where you're already building your project, not a new one, because it needs to see what you have. When it hands back the files, check one thing yourself before accepting anything. Confirm that no variable name starts with NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ if it's a real key. You check that yourself, even if it tells you everything's fine.
tasks.prompt:
Act as the senior developer responsible for this project's security. I'm about to publish it on the internet and I don't want any key traveling with the files.

Do this, in this order:

1) Go through every file in the project and give me a list of every key, password, token, and database address written directly into the code. Tell me the file and line number for each. If there are none, say so clearly.

2) Create a .env file with all those keys, one per line, in NAME=value format, no quotes and no spaces around the equals sign. Use uppercase names that are self-explanatory.

3) Change the code so it reads each value from the environment instead of having it written in. Show me the before and after of every line you touch.

4) Create a .env.example identical to the .env but with the values replaced by the words your_key_here, and with a comment above each line saying which web address that key comes from.

5) Create or update the .gitignore so it includes .env and all its variants, like .env.local and .env.production. Show me the file's full content.

6) Go through each variable name one by one. If any secret key has a name starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_, warn me IN CAPITAL LETTERS, because that prefix publishes it to every visitor's browser. Rename it and explain what needs to change so the site keeps working by calling from the server.

End by telling me in one sentence what I need to do by hand and what you've already done. Direct, no fluff.
tasks.expect: Three files. A .env with the keys. A .env.example with the same names but blank values. And a .gitignore that contains the line .env. And not a single key written inside the code files.
tasks.stuck: If it tells you that was already set up, ask it to prove it. Write: "show me the literal content of the .gitignore and tell me which line number .env appears on." If it dodges and doesn't show you the content, it wasn't actually set up.

tasks.title: Run an audit on the project before you publish it
tasks.where: In the AI's text box, in a fresh, empty conversation
tasks.action: This one has to happen in a NEW conversation, on purpose. You want it looking with fresh eyes, not defending what it wrote itself twenty messages ago. Upload the project files or paste the content. Always do this task right before publishing, and always after a long session where you've been accepting changes without reading them.
tasks.prompt:
You're an external security auditor. You didn't write this code and you have no stake in defending it. Your only job is to find leaked keys before I publish this on the internet.

Review everything I've given you and answer in exactly this format:

FINDINGS
One line per thing found, with file, line number, what type of key it looks like, and which company issues it. Look at least for these prefixes: sk-, sk-ant-, sk-proj-, sk_live_, pk_live_, AIza, ghp_, github_pat_, xoxb-, eyJ, and also long strings of letters and numbers with no apparent meaning.

IN THE BROWSER
Tell me which files in this project get downloaded to any visitor's computer and whether any key travels inside them. Pay special attention to any variable whose name starts with NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_.

IN THE HISTORY
Tell me if there's a keys file that might have been uploaded before and is still sitting in the version history, and explain how I check that myself.

VERDICT
One of these two sentences and nothing else: "You can publish" or "Don't publish yet."

WHAT I DO NOW
The concrete, ordered steps, starting with the keys that need rotating. For each key that needs rotating, tell me the exact web address where it's rotated.

If you find nothing, write literally "reviewed, zero findings" instead of giving me advice. Don't give me a list of best practices: I don't want it. Be direct, no fluff.
tasks.expect: Either a "reviewed, zero findings" with the verdict to publish, or a list with file and line. If the list shows up, you have work to do: fix the files first, then rotate every key that appears, no exceptions.
tasks.stuck: If it answers with generalities like "remember not to upload secrets to the repository," it hasn't actually looked at the files. Reply: "I don't want advice, I want results. Give me file and line number, or write literally: reviewed, zero findings."

tasks.title: Check it with your own eyes in the browser
tasks.where: In your browser, with your site open in front of you
tasks.action: This task doesn't delegate anything to the AI, and that's exactly why it leaves you the most at ease. Open your site; if you haven't published it yet, open it locally, that address that starts with localhost. Press F12, or right-click and "Inspect." A panel full of tabs opens. Go to "Sources" in Chrome, or "Debugger" in Firefox. There it is, file by file, everything your site sends to the computer of whoever visits it. Now press Ctrl+Shift+F (Cmd+Option+F on Mac): that shortcut searches inside all those files at once. Search for five things, one at a time: sk-, AIza, api_key, secret, and password.
tasks.expect: Zero results across all five searches. If something shows up, click the result and read it. It could be your real key, or it could just be that word written in a comment. You only know by looking at it.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the "Sources" tab, use the simpler shortcut. On the page press Ctrl+U (view source) and then Ctrl+F to search for sk- and AIza in there. It covers less, but catches the most common case. And if a key shows up, don't start fixing the code: go rotate it first, that's the next task, and fix it afterward.

tasks.title: Run a rotation drill with the key you just got
tasks.action: You're going to break a key on purpose, calmly, with nothing at stake. That way, the day it happens for real, you'll already have done it once. The order matters, don't skip it. One: create a new key with "Create API key," without touching the old one yet. Two: save it in your password manager with today's date. Three: if the old one was set anywhere (a .env, the Vercel panel, some tool), replace it there and check everything still works. Four, and only then: go back to the key list, find the old one, and click the trash icon. That last step is irreversible, and that's exactly the point. The second you delete it, anything still using it stops working.
tasks.expect: One key fewer and one key more in the list, and your project working just like before. Time yourself: the first time it's about three minutes. Knowing it's three minutes is exactly what's going to take the panic out of the bad day.
tasks.stuck: If something stops working after you delete the old one, breathe: it means there was a spot you missed updating, and now you know which one it was. Go to that spot, paste in the new key, and you're done. Discovering this today in a drill is infinitely better than discovering it with the house on fire. If you don't see the trash icon, you're on the summary view. Click the project name to get into the key's detail page.

tasks.title: Write your leak protocol and put it somewhere you'll find it
tasks.where: In the AI's text box, then in your notes document
tasks.action: The day a key leaks you're going to be nervous and you won't think clearly. That's why this gets written today and not that day. Paste the prompt, keep what comes out, and save it in the same document where you keep your prompts. It needs to fit on your phone screen without scrolling.
tasks.prompt:
I want to write an emergency card for the day one of my API keys leaks. I need to be able to read it and act on it while nervous, without having to think.

Here are the keys I use right now:
[LIST YOUR KEYS: COMPANY AND WHAT YOU USE IT FOR. FOR EXAMPLE: Google Gemini, for my site's chat / Supabase, for the database]

And here's where they're pasted:
[LIST WHERE THEY LIVE: my .env file on my computer / the Vercel panel / such-and-such tool. IF YOU DON'T KNOW, WRITE: I don't know]

Write me the protocol in a maximum of seven numbered lines. Each line starts with an imperative verb and describes a single action. Inside each line, include the exact web address where that action is done. Order them by what has to happen first, and the very first thing has to be stopping the damage, not understanding what happened.

You must include: where to create a new key for each provider I use, where to delete the old one, where I check usage to see if money was spent, and what email address I write to if usage is high.

Don't include: prevention tips, explanations of why it happened, or anything that isn't an action I can carry out in under two minutes. Plain text so I can copy it into my notes.
tasks.expect: Between five and seven lines, each starting with a verb, with the web addresses included right inside the line itself. No paragraphs.
tasks.stuck: If you get a whole page of explanations, reply: "too long. Maximum seven lines, one action per line, with the web addresses inside. I'm going to be reading this with shaking hands."

tasks.title: Tell the AI, permanently, how to treat your keys
tasks.where: In ChatGPT's custom instructions, Claude's preferences, or your project's instructions
tasks.action: In ChatGPT: your photo at the top right, "Personalization," then "Custom instructions." In Claude: your name at the bottom left, "Settings," then "Profile"; or inside a project, "Set project instructions." In Gemini: "Saved info." Paste the text below there, in settings, not in a conversation. That way it applies to everything and you never have to repeat it. It's short on purpose: what you put there affects absolutely everything you do, so don't pile more onto it.
tasks.prompt: When you write code for me, never write a key, password, or token directly into a code file. Always put them in a .env file, make the code read them from there, and make sure the .gitignore includes .env. Never use the NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ prefix for a secret key; if you think it's needed, stop and explain why before writing it. If I ever paste a key into the chat, warn me in the first line of your reply that I need to rotate it and give me the exact web address where it's rotated. And never ask me to paste a key to you: you don't need it to write code.
tasks.expect: The text saved on the settings screen, not in a conversation. To check it's taken effect, open a new conversation and ask for anything that uses a key. It should set up the .env without you having to ask.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find where permanent instructions are saved, don't waste half an hour looking: paste that same text at the start of every new project instead. It works just as well, you just have to remember to do it.

matters: Actually rotating, not just deleting the line from the file. This is the mistake that turns a scare into a bill. You delete the key from the code and relax. But the key is still alive on the company's servers and stored in GitHub's history, working great for whoever copied it.

Checking the name's prefix before publishing. A variable starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ gets sent to every visitor's browser by design. That thirteen-character detail is the entire difference between a normal site and a key published on the internet for anyone to see.
Setting the spending cap before writing the first line. After the leak it's useless, and it's literally the only thing separating losing $10 from losing $1,900.

Never pasting the key into the chat box. The AI doesn't need it to write your code. And in exchange it stays saved in a conversation. That conversation can be shared with a link, exported to a file, or sit in your history for years waiting.
ignore: Professional secrets managers: HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Doppler. These are built for teams of fifteen people with different keys per environment. A well-set-up .env and your hosting panel do the same job while it's just you.

Encrypting the .env file itself with tools like SOPS or git-crypt. It makes sense the day you need to share keys with a team through GitHub. If you're not sharing them with anyone, it adds steps and adds no security.
The difference between OAuth, JWT, refresh tokens, and API keys. These are four different ways of proving who you are to a service, and you're only going to touch the fourth one for quite a while.
canDo: Find keys written inside the code if you show it the files. It's fast and thorough at recognizing prefixes, and it catches things you'd miss simply because you don't yet know what they look like.
Set up the .env, .env.example, and .gitignore correctly on the first try. And rewrite the code so it reads keys from there instead of having them written in.

Translate errors for you. If you paste the full message, it tells you what kind of error it is. A 401 means the key is mistyped or the program isn't reading it. A 403 means the key is valid but doesn't have permission for that. A 429 means you've hit the call limit or run out of credit.
Write your emergency protocol and your permanent instructions. It's paperwork that would take you an hour to draft well and that it hands you finished in twenty seconds.
cantDo: It can't see your .env file, your Vercel panel, or your key list unless you show it to it. When it tells you "I've checked and your .env is correct," it's imagining that.
It doesn't know if your key is already leaked. It doesn't check leak databases or scan GitHub: that's done by other, different programs, and it doesn't talk to them.
It can't rotate the key for you. That button is on the company's website, behind your password, and has to be pressed with your own finger.
It can't really clean GitHub's history. It'll give you a command that looks like it does. But copies bots already grabbed can't be deleted by anyone. That's why rotating is the only fix that exists.
words: API key
A long string of letters and numbers a program shows to prove it has permission. Whoever holds it can spend under your name without anyone asking anything else.
Environment variable
A piece of data that lives outside the program, stored separately, that the program fetches when it needs it. It exists so that data isn't written inside the code and doesn't travel with it anywhere.
.env
A text file in your project folder where you write your keys, one per line. It's the only place in the project where a full key should be written.
.gitignore
A list of file names that don't get uploaded to the internet when you push your project. If the keys file is on that list, it stays on your computer and never leaves.
Rotate
Creating a new key and deleting the old one, so the old one stops working entirely. It's the only way to fix a key that's been exposed.
Repository
Your project's folder stored on the internet, almost always on GitHub, with every previous version of every file. If it's public, anyone can read it, including the versions you thought you'd deleted.
Frontend
The part of your site that downloads entirely to the computer of whoever visits it. Anything you put there can be read by any visitor in two keystrokes, even with zero technical knowledge.
Bot
A program that works alone, with no one watching, repeating a task nonstop. The ones that hunt for keys don't rest, don't get bored, and scan millions of pages a day.
Prefix
The first characters of a text string. In keys they indicate which company issued them, and they're exactly the first thing programs scanning the internet look for.
Spending cap
The maximum amount you allow a company to charge you in a month. Once that number is hit, the service cuts off instead of continuing to add up.
